content: The case studies on HIV testing services will be utilized to highlight successful programs and may be included in the forthcoming Consolidated Guidelines on HIV Testing Services, which are scheduled for release in December 2018. Each case study should be concise, limited to 1–2 pages, and may include photographs to enhance its appeal. The submission deadline for these case studies is May 15, 2019. To make the case studies more relatable to healthcare providers, contributors are encouraged to include one or two high-resolution images (at least 300 dpi) that illustrate the program. If identifiable individuals are featured in the images, written consent must be provided for each individual. The case studies should be approximately 400 words in length and structured under specific subheadings, including: 1. Target Population and Context: This should describe the key populations served (e.g., men who have sex with men, sex workers, people in prisons, people who inject drugs, transgender individuals, or combinations of these groups), the country or region of implementation, and the setting of the program (e.g., home-based, school, workplace, mobile, or index testing). It should also explain how users are linked to further HIV testing and care, the program’s specific aims (including development-related goals), and the program’s start date and relevant data collection dates. 2. Key Methodologies: This section should detail the methods used to develop, implement, and evaluate the HIV testing program. It should include methodologies for program development, reaching the target population, monitoring and evaluating outcomes (including data collection methods), developing national policies and regulatory frameworks, and implementing monitoring systems such as preand post-market surveillance or community-based monitoring to identify adverse events or harm. 3. This should include preand post-intervention data, such as background HIV prevalence or incidence in the tested population, HIV testing uptake, and testing frequency. It should also report the number and percentage of individuals with reactive test results, confirmed HIV-positive diagnoses, and those linked to treatment and care. Additionally, it should report the number and percentage of individuals with non-reactive test results who were linked to healthcare and HIV prevention services (e.g. The presence or absence of policies supporting the integration of HIV testing services with tuberculosis or family planning services should also be noted, along with reasons for the program’s success, challenges, and additional evidence from monitoring and evaluation. The case studies will be scored using a tool developed by the HIV Testing Services (HTS) guideline steering committee. Strong case studies should clearly describe the program setting, methods used to reach the target population, and any innovations. They should present program data, including client access to HIV testing services, the number of positive results, linkage to prevention and treatment, and client satisfaction. Evidence of program successes or challenges, as well as approaches targeting key populations or other vulnerable groups not yet reached, should also be included. The quality of each case study will be rated on a scale from 1 (poor) to 5 (very good). Reviewers may request clarifications or additional information if needed. The importance of the case study’s subject matter in the context of the new HTS guidelines will also be assessed, with ratings ranging from 1 (unimportant) to 5 (very important). Thematic areas of importance include service integration and programmatic linkages (e.g., HIV and other diseases such as STIs, TB, and hepatitis), assisted partner notification services, demand creation for HIV testing, risk-based or symptom screening tools, multiplex testing (e.g., HIV/syphilis dual tests), recency assays, quality assurance, retesting, and other relevant areas. Selected case studies may be published in the main body of the guideline chapters or included in an annex. If the content of a case study is promising but requires improvement in writing, the review team may collaborate with the authors to enhance clarity.
